latin: Mihi ignosce, Domne, ubi veneunt<sup>1</sup> crepundia<sup>2</sup>?
Cujuslibet generis crepundia in tabulato tertio invenietis.
Nolite hac<sup>3</sup> transire, Domnae! Potius per scalas mechanicas conscendite!
Ecce crepundiorum locus! Pretii modici munus<sup>4</sup> quaerimus.
Puerone an puellae dabitur<sup>5</sup> hoc munus?
Filio meo id donare volo.
Quot annos natus est?
Novem annorum est.
Visne ludicrum constructivum<sup>6</sup> ligneum? tubam aeream<sup>7</sup>? tympanum<sup>8</sup>?
Ludicrum illud ei non placebit; tuba autem et tympanum mihi displicent.
Hoc tramine<sup>9</sup> electrico delectabitur, vel illa nave<sup>10</sup> cum velis.
Quanti constant?
Pretium traminis HS (sestertiis)<sup>11</sup> septemdecim, navis novem.
Haec munera pulchra sed cara sunt. Filio globulos emam<sup>12</sup>.
At ego filiae pupam<sup>13</sup> comparabo<sup>14</sup>.
Globulos hic quoque habemus. Puparum locus haud procul<sup>15</sup> distat.
english: Excuse me, sir, where are toys (rattles) sold?
You[pl.] will find toys of all kinds (of whatever kind you like) on the third floor.
Don't come (cross) through here (by this [way]), Ladies! Use the escalator instead (rather go up through the mechanical stairs).
Here's the toy department (behold the place of rattles). We are looking for a moderately priced present (gift of moderate price).
Will the present be given to a boy or girl?
I want to present my son with it (it to my son).
How old is he (how many years has he been born)?
He is nine (he is of nine years).
Do you want a wooden construction set (wooden constructive toy)? a copper trumpet? a drum?
He will not like that toy (that plaything will not please him). The trumpet and the drum, on the other hand, I do not like (displease me).
He will be delighted by this electric train or-if-you-prefer by that sailing ship (ship with sails).
How much do they cost?
The price of the train, 17 dollars (sesterces); of the ship, 9.
These gifts are nice (beautiful) but expensive. I will buy my son (to my son) marbles.
And I will get a doll for my daughter.
We also have marbles here. The dolls section (place of dolls) is not far away.

footnotes: Veneo, -is, -ire, to be sold; an irregular verb conjugated like ire, to go.
Crepundia, -orum, n., toys [really rattle]; this 2nd declension neuter noun is used only in the plural.
Hác, through here (place through which one passes) Do not forget the long á!
Munus, -eris, n., gift (has other senses which we shall see later). Another (neuter) noun in -us of the 3rd declension.
Dabitur: pass. future of dare, to give (general sense); donare, to make a gift, a present.
Constructivus, -a, -um, adj., derived from construere, to build.
Æreus, -a, -um, of copper (brass) or more precisely of bronze, an alloy containing copper (and tin).
Tympanum, -i, n., drum or tympanum (in all senses of these words, that is to say a round membrane or body of scant thickness).
Tramen, -inis, n., the train, a word of recent creation coming (as the English word “train”) from trahere, to drag (Fr., traîner).
Navis, -is, f., gen. pl. navium, is one of those parisyllabics of which we will talk again next week.

Sestertius, -ii, m., sesterce (Roman currency). Its symbol HS seems to have that of the American dollar ($), hence the daring translation we have allowed ourselves! This currency having been devalued, the “heavy sesterce” (sestertium, -ii) was also used, which is worth a thousand “light sesterces”!
Emam: future of emere, to buy. Globulus, -i, m., the marble, diminutive of globus, -i, m., the sphere, the globe.
Pupa. Do we still need to tell you that this word belongs to the 1st declension?: pupa, -ae, f., the doll.
Comparare, to get hold of, to buy (cum + parare) gave rise to the Italian comprare (and also comperare), to buy.
Procul, adv., far. Haud is a negative adverb, but which negates only the following word, whereas non negates the entire clause.
comments: Let us take advantage of the fact that the lesson is short to put our knowledge about adjectives in order.
The declension of adjectives.— Adjectives are divided into two classes:
1. The 1st class borrows its forms from the 1st and 2nd declension:
— masculine in -us or -er		gen. in -i	(2nd decl.)
— feminine in -a			gen. in -ae	(1st decl.)
— neuter in -um			gen. in -i	(2nd decl.)
Ex.:	bonus medicus, the good doctor;
bona raeda, the good car;
bonum remedium, the good remedy (medicine).
2. The second class borrows all its forms from the third declension: therefore, these vary greatly in the nominative, but, of course, the genitive is always in -is.
a) parisyllabics:
nom.	gravis homo	gravis femina	grave onus
the serious person	the serious woman	the heavy burden (neuter)
gen.	gravis hominis	gravis feminae	gravis oneris
abl.	gravi homine	gravi feminá	gravi onere
gen. pl.	gravium hominum	gravium feminarum	gravium onerum
b) imparisyllabics:
nom.	ingens equus	ingens locusta	ingens plaustrum
the huge horse	the huge lobster	the huge wagon (neuter)
gen.	ingentis equi	ingentis locustae	ingentis plaustri
abl.	ingenti equo	ingenti locustá	ingenti plaustro
gen. pl.	ingentium equorum	ingentium locustarum	ingentium plaustrorum

The declension of the adjectives of the 2nd class is even simpler than that of the nouns of the third declension: the ablative is almost always in -i, instead of -e, and the genitive plural in -ium. But there are some exceptions, such as vetus (old), gen. veteris, abl. vetere and gen. pl. veterum.
For the moment do not be surprised if you find one or the other form and wait until all that clears up through use.

latin: Periit gallus proh dolor! (bis)
Numquam canet sic cirici cirici,
Nec sonabit vox cocori cococo.
Nec sonabit vox cocori coco!
english: The rooster perished, oh, sorrow! (twice)
Never will it sing thus: cock-a-doodle-doo, cock-a-doodle-doo (kee-ree-kee, kee-ree-kee),
Nor will [its] voice sound: cock-a-doodle-doo, cock-a-doodle-doo (ko-ko-ree ko-ko-ko).
Nor will [its] voice sound: cock-a-doodle-doo, cock-a-doodle-doo (ko-ko-ree ko-ko)!
